How Much Wattage Does Your GPU Actually Need?

The graphics card sets the size of the PSU. The CPU matters too, but a modern gaming processor draws far less than the card under a gaming load. Use the GPU maker’s recommended system wattage as your floor, then add headroom.

  • Entry cards (RTX 5060 class, integrated graphics): a quality 550W to 650W unit is plenty.
  • RTX 5070 class: NVIDIA recommends a 650W system power supply. We fit 750W so the PSU never runs near its limit.
  • RTX 5070 Ti and RX 9070 XT class: 750W is the realistic minimum; 850W gives comfortable headroom.
  • RTX 5080 class: NVIDIA recommends 850W. An 850W Gold unit is the sensible choice.
  • RTX 5090 class: NVIDIA recommends 1000W. We prefer 1000W to 1200W, especially with a 16-core CPU.

If you are still choosing the card itself, browse our graphics cards first and size the power supply afterwards.

Why headroom matters

Modern graphics cards produce short power spikes well above their average draw. A PSU that is already near its rated load can trip its protection during those spikes, which looks like a random shutdown or black screen in the middle of a game. Running a unit at around 50 to 70 percent of its rating keeps it in its most efficient range and keeps the fan slow.

ATX 3.0, ATX 3.1 and the 12V-2x6 Connector

Newer NVIDIA cards use a single 16-pin connector (12V-2x6, the updated version of 12VHPWR) instead of several 8-pin plugs. ATX 3.0 and ATX 3.1 power supplies ship with this cable natively, so there is no adapter hanging off the card.

A native cable matters more than people think. Adapters add bulk, bend the connector at awkward angles and make it easier to leave the plug partly seated. If you are buying an RTX 50-series card, an ATX 3.x unit such as the NZXT C850, DeepCool PL750D or DeepCool PQ1000G is the cleaner option. Push the connector in until it clicks and avoid sharp bends right at the plug.

Bronze vs Gold: What the Rating Means

The 80 PLUS rating describes efficiency: how much of the power drawn from the wall reaches your components instead of turning into heat. Gold units waste less energy than Bronze units at the same load.

In practice, the efficiency gap alone will not change your electricity bill much. The real reasons to choose Gold are indirect. Gold units are usually built with better capacitors, run cooler and are more often fully modular, which makes cable management and airflow easier inside your PC case. Bronze is fine for budget and office builds; Gold is what we fit in most gaming systems.

Buying a PSU for Bahrain’s Climate

Ambient temperature in Bahrain stays high for much of the year, and many PCs sit in rooms where the air conditioning cycles on and off. Heat shortens component life, and power supplies are no exception. A few habits help:

  • Mount the PSU fan facing down if the case has a filtered bottom vent, so it pulls cool air from outside the case.
  • Clean the dust filter every few weeks; desert dust builds up faster than most people expect.
  • Choose more headroom rather than less. A unit loafing at half load stays cooler in a hot room.
  • Use a quality surge protector or UPS, especially for workstations doing long renders.

Common Power Supply Mistakes We See

Most PSU problems that reach our bench fall into a few patterns:

  1. Reusing an old unit with a new card. A five-year-old PSU may have the wattage on paper but not the connectors or the transient handling a new GPU needs.
  2. Buying on wattage alone. A cheap high-wattage unit is not the same as a quality unit of slightly lower wattage.
  3. Daisy-chaining PCIe cables. On cards with several 8-pin inputs, use separate cables from the PSU where possible.
  4. Ignoring the case length. Large 1000W and 1200W units are longer. Check the case clearance before ordering.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the power supply price in Bahrain for a gaming PC?

At Grey PC, a reliable 750W unit for a mid-range gaming PC costs about 28 to 35 BHD. An 850W Gold unit for an RTX 5070 Ti or RTX 5080 costs around 50 to 55 BHD, and a 1000W Gold unit for flagship cards is about 60 BHD. Prices change with stock, so check the PSU category for current figures.

Is a 750W PSU enough for an RTX 5070?

Yes. NVIDIA recommends a 650W system power supply for the RTX 5070, so a quality 750W unit gives comfortable headroom for power spikes and a future CPU upgrade. Choose an ATX 3.0 or 3.1 unit so you get a native 16-pin cable instead of an adapter.

What PSU do I need for an RTX 5080?

NVIDIA recommends 850W for the RTX 5080, and that is what we fit. An 850W Gold, ATX 3.x unit such as the NZXT C850 or Darkflash PMT850 handles the card and a high-end gaming CPU with room to spare. Pair it with a case that has good front intake airflow.

Is a Gold PSU worth it over Bronze?

For most gaming builds, yes. At the same wattage, Gold units usually cost only 5 to 7 BHD more than Bronze. They run cooler and quieter and are more often fully modular, which helps airflow. For a basic office PC, a good Bronze unit is perfectly adequate.

Can I reuse my old power supply with a new graphics card?

Sometimes, but check three things first: the wattage, the connectors the new card needs, and the age of the unit. Older units often lack the 16-pin connector and may not handle the short power spikes of modern GPUs. If the PSU is more than five years old, replacing it is the safer choice.
